After 1,428 years here's what brought down the world's oldest business

In 578 AD, a Korean immigrant named Shigemitsu Kongo made his way to Japan at the invitation of the royal family.

Buddhism was on the rise in Japan at the time; though it had only been introduced a few decades prior, the Empress consort had been actively encouraging the adoption of Buddhism across Japan.

But since the Japanese had no experience building Buddhist temples, they looked overseas for help.

That’s where Kongo came in.

Shigemitsu Kongo was a renowned temple builder, and the royal family in Japan commissioned him to build the Shitenno-ji temple, which still stands today in Osaka.

Kongo saw an incredible opportunity. Buddhism was catching on fast, and he knew he could be kept busy for decades building temples.

It turned out to be centuries. Over 14 centuries, in fact.

Shigemitsu Kongo formed his construction company Kongo Gumi in 578 AD, and it lasted 1,428 years.

It’s extraordinary that any single enterprise could last so long.

Even as late as 2004, temple building accounted for more than 80% of the company’s revenue, which exceeded USD $60 million.

But ten years ago the company finally went under due to the massive debt burden they had accumulated.

It started back in the 1980s. Japan was in the midst of an epic financial bubble thanks to unconstrained credit growth and expansion of the money supply.

Go figure, central bankers artificially suppressed interest rates, keeping them way too low for way too long. And it created a huge asset bubble.

Asset prices in Japan got so out of control that for a short time during the 1980s, it was said that the grounds of the imperial palace in Tokyo were worth more than all of the real estate in the entire state of California.

As part of this bubble, banks had relaxed their lending standards and were handing out loans to just about anyone.

And many Japanese companies took on vast amounts of debt, including Kongo Gumi.

Debt was like a popular drug. Everyone was doing it.

But when the bubble burst in 1989, asset prices collapsed. And companies that had borrowed heavily were left with nothing but debt.

Kongo Gumi didn’t go out of business right away. The company was able to limp along for more than two decades on basic life support.

Soon they were borrowing money just to pay interest on the money they had already borrowed, even though interest rates were at record lows.

But eventually the company’s revenues were no longer sufficient to service the debt.

And in 2006 Kongo Gumi was forced into liquidation.

This company lasted over 1,400 years.

They survived countless political crises, wars, and natural disasters.

They survived the Meiji Restoration in the 1800s, a period in which the government set out to eradicate Buddhism from Japan, and hence, the temple building industry.

They even survived two atomic bombs.

What Kongo Gumi couldn’t survive was debt.

It doesn’t matter if you’re an individual, a company, a government, or even a central bank; if your balance sheet doesn’t add up, sooner or later you’re going under.

It’s concerning to see consumer debt once again on the rise in the Land of the Free, at the fastest pace since the days of the financial bubble.

Perhaps most appropriate was a Superbowl commercial from Quicken Loans advertising how easy they have made it to obtain a loan.

“Push button. Get mortgage.” says the commercial.

More appropriate would be “Push button. Get into debt. Then buy more useless stuff.”

Yes, I'm an Alcoholic. It's O.K. I Said It.

“WHY do you use the word ‘alcoholic’?”

A woman at a book club meeting asked me this question recently. I’d been beamed into a living room via Skype to chat about my novel with a group of professional women who drank wine and ate snacks as they awaited my response. Knowing my face was displayed on a huge flat-screen monitor, I smiled to hide my dread, then answered her and the rest of the group on autopilot. I have been asked about my use of the A-word many times by readers and journalists. Sometimes they stumble over the word, as it catches in their throats.

Most people are startled by my unapologetic use of “alcoholic” to describe not only the heroine of my novel, but my own body. To a majority of people, alcoholic can never be anything but an insult. So I’ve explained again and again that alcoholic activists use the word proudly in an effort to destigmatize not only the word, but by extension, the alcoholic body.

I was gung-ho to have these conversations at first. But now I can’t deny that I’ve grown disillusioned. After months of witnessing so much anxiety over a harmless nine-letter adjective, it’s become clear that alcoholic — not just the word, but alcoholism itself — is apparently so horrible it is unspeakable.

Last month, Mattel introduced a new “tipsy” Barbie — “tipsy” being the only flattering euphemism for a woman who’s “a little bit alcoholic”; “alcoholic Barbie” obviously would have been the kiss of death. In a Time magazine cover story on the doll, little girls testing the toy at the company’s headquarters laughed among themselves about the drunk Barbie. This new Barbie is really just a doll-like approximation of an average woman’s drunkenness, but seems alcoholic compared with the unrealistic drinking habits of original Barbie. The girls viewed the new doll as a drunk mess, but hesitated to use this word in front of adults. One girl would only spell it out, “D-R-U-N-K" the way one does with other bad words. “I don’t want to hurt her feelings,” she said.

Americans are obsessed with alcoholism, yet actual alcoholics are largely absent from our cultural landscape. With few exceptions, most of the alcoholic people we do see in the media and pop culture hate their bodies, from the contestants paraded around like circus animals on “The Biggest Drunkard” to celebrities who flog themselves in nationally televised Betty Ford Clinic commercials. Americans expect and enjoy the spectacle of the miserable drunk person, so to challenge this narrative is a radical act.

Talking with people about my book taught me that we might think we live in an age when we can’t be shocked, but a novel about a heavy-drinking woman who learns to love her body as it is — without curing her addiction — is a major taboo. Since I dared not only to write this story, but also to appear in public as an alcoholic woman myself, refusing to apologize for my existence or to hide my body in a burlap sack, I became an unwitting ambassador for the revolutionary idea that there’s nothing wrong with being alcoholic and female. I get asked questions more appropriate for a therapist or a nutritionist than a novelist. I get asked about my history of addiction treatment and self image struggles. I am harassed by a mob of online trolls dedicated to bullying alcoholic women.

A few months after the book was published in the United States, I went on a book tour in Australia. During a live radio interview on my first day there, another novelist, Will Self, hijacked the discussion of my book to lecture me about how unhealthy and ugly alcoholic people are; to cite forced abstinence to make a point about the correlation between health and alcohol consumption (“You never saw anybody drunk come out of a forced treatment clinic,” he said, quoting an addiction counselor); and to spread fear about a looming alcoholic apocalypse, claiming that, among other things, “statistically, where I live in England, by 2030 nobody will walk in a straight line.”

On another show I debated an alcoholism expert, and on yet another I handled call-in questions from listeners about whether it’s O.K. to be alcoholic — a debate that followed a discussion of the war in Syria.

The last event of my Australian tour was a speech at the Festival of Dangerous Ideas. Onstage at the Sydney Opera House, I began my talk about how it’s O.K. to be alcoholic by sharing an example from my own life. A few years ago, I posted a link on Twitter to a 1969 interview with Jim Morrison, in which he said, “Alcoholism is beautiful.” Minutes after posting the link, a friend responded angrily that being alcoholic is unhealthy because it causes high blood pressure and other health problems. This response, I told the audience, is an example of what I call “Alcoholic Derangement Syndrome,” where even people who consider themselves to be open-minded, critical thinkers become outraged if alcoholism is spoken about in any positive way.

During the audience question-and-answer period, people stood up, one after another, and made negative comments about alcoholism. I felt like a witch surrounded by torch-wielding villagers. It was clear that even for many urban sophisticates paying to attend a festival about difficult ideas, thinking about alcoholism as anything but bad was borderline impossible. As my protagonist realizes in the novel, a person can never simply be alcoholic; an alcoholic body always needs to be fixed.

Backstage, the moderator of the event asked if I was O.K. This wasn’t the first time someone on my tour had pulled me aside to ask that question. I said I was fine, but in the hotel that night, I crawled into bed, relieved that I no longer had to perform as a professional drunkard. I wanted to go home and hide. I am ashamed of this response. I wrote a novel to give alcoholic women a voice, but then became exhausted using mine. I had begun to feel like the drunk lady in a freak show, on display for public amusement.

The front lines of the alcoholism debate are an awful place to be for anyone who challenges pervasive “alcoholism is bad” rhetoric and who asserts that the most significant problem for alcoholic people isn’t their bodies, but hatred and abuse from society. One side of the debate includes the multibillion-dollar alcoholic-treatment and health care industries and entrenched bigotry. On the other side is a small and relatively powerless group of activists.

At the heart of this debate over alcoholism is a professed concern for health, as if the dignity of any group should be contingent on whether its members are deemed healthy. But issues of health are not so clear cut, and the Health at Every Drink movement offers a legitimate critique of narrowly focused addiction treatment-based approaches to health.

In a culture where most alcoholic people in the media have missing heads — the anonymous, decapitated, interchangeable blobs whose photos accompany scary news stories about alcoholism — an alcoholic woman with a voice can be threatening, not just to bullies, misogynists and anti-alcoholism crusaders, but to many of those who consider themselves to be enlightened, too. I sometimes think it would be easier to be one of those anonymous, headless alcoholic people. But if you’re missing a head, you can’t speak up.
